titleEn: Confused and Hypotensive at 82 - Suspected Sepsis From a Urinary Source

patient.name: Dorothy Pearce
patient.affectEn: slumped in her recliner, eyes half open, mumbling; drowsy and drifts off between answers; face flushed; breathing fast; does not try to get up. Later in the call she becomes harder to rouse and her words stop making sense.
patient.speechEn: mumbled fragments ("I'm fine dear... I'm fine"); cannot say where she is or what year it is; when asked directly about pain she points to her lower belly. Most of the history comes from the care aide.

scene.settingEn: Assisted-living residence in Nanaimo, 1420 hrs. Clean, warm suite, adequate lighting, no hazards. One patient: an 82-year-old woman slumped in her recliner, eyes half open, mumbling. A care aide is with her and has the full medication list. Strong smell of urine; her incontinence pad is soaked. Her walker is beside the chair; full drink glasses sit untouched on the side table. Nanaimo Regional General Hospital is 8 minutes away; the nearest PCP car is 15 minutes out.

bystanders.knowsEn: BASELINE: she is normally fully oriented and independent with a walker, and does her own crossword every morning; she has mild memory problems but is oriented. She was her usual self yesterday. Over the last two days she has been going to the toilet more often, complaining of burning, and eating and drinking almost nothing; last night she was up all night; this morning she was confused and had an unwitnessed fall in the bathroom - nobody knows whether she hit her head. No cough, no shortness-of-breath complaint, no chest pain, no vomiting, no diarrhea. She has had "water infections" twice before, and the last one also made her confused. PMHx: high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis, mild cognitive impairment but oriented. Meds (full list from the nursing station): apixaban, bisoprolol, acetaminophen as needed. Allergy: sulfa - rash. LOI: a few sips of tea this morning, no solid food for 24 hours. Does not know her weight. Will hand over the medication list if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
hard collars, head blocks and a spinal immobilization device
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline, D10W, dimenhydrinate, ondansetron

dispatchEn: 1420 hrs. Code 3 to an assisted-living residence in Nanaimo. Staff report an 82-year-old woman is 'not herself' - confused since this morning, will not get out of her chair, and feels hot to touch. Nanaimo Regional General Hospital is 8 minutes away; the nearest PCP car is 15 minutes out.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: staff say she was her usual self yesterday. She has been drinking very little for two days and has had one unwitnessed fall in her suite this morning. There is a full medication list at the nursing station.
arrivalEn: A care aide meets you at the door of a clean, warm suite with the medication list in her hand: "She's not herself today." Adequate lighting, no hazards. One patient.
firstLookEn: An elderly woman slumped in a recliner, eyes half open, mumbling. Her face is flushed and she is breathing fast. There is a strong smell of urine and her incontinence pad is soaked. Full drink glasses sit untouched on the side table; her walker is beside the chair.

primary.locEn: Opens her eyes to your voice, mumbles "I'm fine dear... I'm fine" and drifts off again. She cannot tell you where she is or what year it is - disoriented (AVPU = V).
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 26, shallow. Clear air entry on both sides.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 116, weak, regular. Hands and feet cool and mottled; capillary refill 4 seconds. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Small bruise on the left hip from the morning fall. No head injury found. No midline neck tenderness; she moves all four limbs on command. Chest non-tender. Abdomen non-tender except the suprapubic area, which is tender to gentle palpation. No external bleeding. Strong smell of urine, soaked incontinence pad. Skin hot and flushed on the trunk, cool and mottled at the hands and feet (skin is given automatically during the RBS).
primary.skinEn: trunk hot and flushed; hands and feet cool and mottled; capillary refill 4 seconds

history.ccEn: Patient: "I'm fine, dear... I'm fine." Care aide: "She's not herself. She's been confused since this morning, she won't get out of her chair, and she feels hot."

opqrst.oEn: Care aide: "She was her usual self yesterday. This morning she was confused - and she had a fall in the bathroom that nobody saw."
opqrst.qEn: Care aide: "She's muddled. She doesn't know where she is - she's normally completely with it."
opqrst.rEn: (Patient, if asked directly where it hurts:) she points to her lower belly: "Down... here..."
opqrst.sEn: (Patient:) "Sore... down there..." She cannot give a number.
opqrst.tEn: Care aide: "Two days of going to the toilet a lot and burning, and hardly eating or drinking. Up all night last night. Confused since this morning."

history.painScoreEn: When asked directly about pain she points to her lower belly and says "Sore... down there"; she cannot give a number.

sample.sEn: Care aide: "Burning and going to the toilet more for two days, hardly eating or drinking, up all night, confused this morning, and she feels hot."
sample.aEn: Care aide: "Sulfa - it gives her a rash."
sample.mEn: Care aide: "Apixaban, bisoprolol, and acetaminophen when she needs it. Here's the full list from the nursing station."
sample.pEn: Care aide: "High blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis, and some mild memory problems - but she's oriented, she does her crossword every morning. She's had water infections twice before, and the last one made her confused too."
sample.lEn: Care aide: "A few sips of tea this morning. No solid food for about 24 hours."
sample.eEn: Care aide: "She fell in the bathroom this morning. Nobody saw it, so we don't know if she hit her head. She's been in her recliner since and won't get up."

fe.generalEn: Care aide: "She's normally independent with her walker and sharp for her age. It's all changed over the last two days."
fe.cnsEn: Care aide: "Just the confusion. No weakness on one side, her face isn't drooping, and her speech is only muddled."
fe.respiratoryEn: Care aide: "No cough, no phlegm, no pain when she breathes."
fe.cardiovascularEn: Care aide: "No chest pain. She has atrial fibrillation - that's not new."
fe.giGuEn: Care aide: "Burning when she pees, going more often, and the urine smells strong. No vomiting, no diarrhea. Her belly only hurts when it's pressed."
fe.integumentaryEn: Care aide: "No rash, no pressure sores. Just the small bruise on her hip from the fall."
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Care aide: "Only the fall this morning. No deformity that I can see."

findings.headNeckEn: No scalp laceration or hematoma; no blood or fluid from the ears or nose. Tongue and lips dry. Neck supple with no midline tenderness, no JVD.
findings.chestLungsEn: Equal air entry, no crackles, no wheeze.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft; tender in the suprapubic region; no rebound, no distension.
findings.backEn: Inspected during the transfer: no pressure sores, no other findings.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Bruise over the left greater trochanter with no shortening or rotation; both legs move on command; pedal pulses weak but present.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Skin tenting on the forearm; cool hands; radial pulses weak but present bilaterally.

resp.character: rapid; clear air entry on both sides

vitalsSets.skin: trunk hot flushed, peripheries cool mottled, CR 4 s

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, about 7 minutes after set 1 - deteriorating (GCS and blood pressure falling); keep her supine, oxygen on, airway protected, update the hospital, keep driving
vitalsSets.skin: trunk hot, hands cold and mottled

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: She is harder to rouse now. She opens her eyes when you speak to her, but her words no longer make sense.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan equipment: oxygen, suction, blood glucose meter, thermometer, blankets, stretcher taken to the patient's room
triggers: bring oxygen, suction, glucometer and thermometer

expected.actionEn: Plan to collect the medication list and, if available, the staff's baseline notes - in a geriatric altered-LOC call the baseline is the single most valuable piece of information
Anticipate the differential before arrival: infection, hypoglycemia, stroke, occult head injury from the unwitnessed fall, medication effect, and dehydration

Verbalize hazards (none), environment (warm indoor room), nature of illness (altered LOC of gradual onset), people (one patient plus a care aide who can give collateral history) and resources (PCP car en route)
triggers: nature of illness is altered LOC

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection; add a mask given an undifferentiated febrile patient
First look: elderly woman, drowsy and mumbling, flushed face, breathing fast, untouched drinks and a soaked pad pointing to poor intake and a urinary source
Assess LOC / AVPU: responds to voice but is disoriented - and compare it against her stated baseline of full orientation, because 'confused' means nothing without a baseline

Apply the NEXUS criteria to the unwitnessed fall and state the conclusion: no midline tenderness, no focal deficit, no intoxication, no distracting injury - but her altered mental status means alertness is NOT normal, so spinal motion restriction is indicated and manual stabilization is taken
Assess the airway and keep suction at hand - her LOC is decreased and she may vomit
Assess breathing: rate 26 and shallow, auscultate both sides - tachypnea in an elderly patient is an early and frequently ignored sign of sepsis
Assess circulation: weak radial pulse of 116 with cool mottled peripheries and 4-second capillary refill - state out loud that this is shock despite the warm flushed trunk
Perform a full rapid body survey, including gentle abdominal and suprapubic palpation to look for the infection source, and check for injuries from the unwitnessed fall
triggers: check for injuries from the fall

expected.actionEn: Identify shock with an altered LOC as a life threat you cannot correct on scene and act on it by shortening scene time
Note the skin: trunk hot and flushed, peripheries cool and mottled
Oxygen to maintain SpO2 at or above 94%: she is at 92% with evidence of shock and an altered LOC, so high-flow oxygen is indicated
Position supine to support blood pressure, and keep her covered - she is hypotensive and moves poorly on her own
Categorize as RTC out loud, citing the altered LOC and the shock findings
Ready to load within 15 minutes, with the secondary survey completed en route
State that definitive care is intravenous fluid and antibiotics at hospital - transport now rather than waiting on scene for the PCP car
Establish the chief complaint: new confusion in a previously oriented 82-year-old, with fever and poor intake
Take the HxC/C from the collateral source: time of onset and rate of change, the baseline mental status, urinary symptoms, oral intake, and the unwitnessed fall including whether the head was struck
triggers: how much has she been drinking

expected.actionEn: Ask about pain despite the confusion: she localizes discomfort to the lower abdomen when asked directly - elderly patients under-report pain
Past medical history, including the two previous urinary infections that also presented as confusion
Medications - the anticoagulant matters twice over: it raises the stakes of the unwitnessed fall, and the beta blocker can blunt the tachycardia you would expect in sepsis
Allergies
Last oral intake - almost nothing for 24 hours, which compounds the hypovolemia
GCS with all three components stated separately and compared to her baseline of 15
Blood pressure by auscultation - recognize 88/52 as hypotension in an 82-year-old whose usual pressure is high
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality - and note that the beta blocker may be masking how tachycardic she should be
Respiratory rate, depth and character with both lung fields auscultated
Skin assessed hands-on centrally and peripherally - the split between a hot trunk and cold hands is the finding
Pupils - size, equality and reaction, important after an unwitnessed fall on an anticoagulant
SpO2 recorded before and after oxygen, with the reading checked against the pulse on a cool peripheral finger
Blood glucose - mandatory in any patient with a decreased level of consciousness
Temperature - indicated in suspected infection; document the route used
FE - General health (the 48-hour trajectory from independent to confused is the story)
FE - CNS (screen for stroke: no facial droop, no unilateral weakness)
FE - Respiratory (pneumonia is the other common septic source in the elderly)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (dysuria, frequency and strong-smelling urine point to the source)
FE - Integumentary (look for cellulitis and pressure sores as alternative sources)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head and neck examined specifically for occult injury from the unwitnessed fall in an anticoagulated patient
Chest auscultated at all six sites, listening for the crackles of a pneumonic source
Abdomen examined in four quadrants with the suprapubic tenderness reported as the likely source
Back examined during the transfer, checking for pressure sores as an alternative source
Upper extremities with skin turgor and bilateral radial pulses documented
Lower extremities: assess the hip after the fall for shortening or rotation, and document pedal pulses

Measure the blood glucose before attributing the altered LOC to infection, and correctly withhold oral glucose and glucagon with a BGL of 9.8 - giving glucose here would be initiating a protocol without indications
triggers: BGL is normal so no glucose

expected.actionEn: Spinal management applied correctly for the unwitnessed fall with altered mental status: manual stabilization, sized hard collar, moved as a unit onto the stretcher, head not taped
Airway management: suction at the head and a plan to tip the whole device if she vomits
Oxygen and positioning per the hypovolemia approach: supine to support blood pressure, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above, kept covered and warm
EMR: Verbalize that IV fluid and antibiotics are outside EMR scope, and that the treatment an EMR controls here is oxygen, position, warmth and speed
triggers: IV fluids are outside my scope

expected.actionEn: Treat her with dignity throughout: explain each step even though she is confused, keep her covered during exposure, and bring the medication list
Reassess ABCs and all interventions after each move and at least every 5 minutes
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes, and interpret the falling GCS with falling blood pressure out loud as worsening septic shock
Protect the airway as the GCS falls: suction in hand, ready to tip the device, ready to assist ventilation if the respirations become inadequate
Keep her supine and covered, and update the receiving hospital with the deterioration rather than stopping to re-examine
En-route notification describing a hypotensive febrile elderly patient with an altered LOC
Complete verbal hand-off including the baseline mental status, the suspected urinary source, the anticoagulant and the unwitnessed fall
Accurate PCR completed within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate initiates c-spine control / spinal motion restriction for the unwitnessed fall (manual stabilization, hard collar, head blocks, spinal device)
candidate asks for or establishes her baseline mental status (what she is normally like) from the aide or the records

candidate actually administers oral glucose, glucagon or D10W although her BGL is 9.8 (record the drug event as well). Asking or deciding whether glucose is indicated, or saying it is withheld, is NOT this event
candidate gives only low-flow oxygen (nasal cannula, or a mask at a low flow) although she is in shock with an altered LOC - high-flow oxygen is required
candidate leaves her sitting up in the recliner, or sits her up for transport, instead of positioning her supine for shock
candidate gives her anything by mouth (drinks, food, tablets, oral glucose) despite her decreased LOC
candidate delays loading or transport to wait for the PCP car, or to start an IV or fluids on scene - vascular access belongs en route
after her GCS and blood pressure fall, the candidate stops or delays transport to repeat the physical examination instead of supporting her and updating the hospital
candidate tapes her head to the spinal device

an EMR-level candidate personally starts an IV or gives IV fluid (outside EMR scope; record the drug event as well). Saying IV fluids are outside EMR scope, or that the PCP or the hospital will give them, is NOT this event
PCP actually starts the fluid bolus before a full baseline set of vital signs (blood pressure, pulse and respirations) has been taken
PCP runs the bolus past 500 mL or onto the next bag without reassessing her (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between
PCP actually gives dimenhydrinate or ondansetron although she has no nausea or vomiting

drugs.doseEn: WITHHELD in this scenario: 15 g PO, repeat at 5 minutes as necessary - only for known or suspected hypoglycemia in a conscious patient with sufficient mentation to maintain her airway. Her BGL is 9.8 and her LOC is decreased: not indicated, and contraindicated.
WITHHELD in this scenario: 0.5-1 mg IM or 3 mg IN for hypoglycemia only. Her BGL is 9.8 - not indicated.
WITHHELD in this scenario (PCP): 10-25 g (100-250 mL of 10% solution) IV only for confirmed hypoglycemia. Her BGL is 9.8.

PCP: vascular access en route; fluid bolus 20 mL/kg IV to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing every 500 mL, target systolic 90 mmHg (hypotensive with clinical signs of shock and 24 hours of almost no intake). Her weight is not known on scene.
PCP: 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg IM, or IV diluted over 1-2 minutes - only if she becomes nauseated or vomits; caution in the elderly. Not indicated in this scenario (no nausea or vomiting).
PCP: 4 mg PO (adult) - only for moderate to severe nausea or vomiting; monitor for CNS effects in the elderly. Not indicated in this scenario (no nausea or vomiting).

C-spine control taken late, or out of sequence with potentially negative consequences, including pain stimulus prior to C-spine control, and/or
Improper strapping not detrimental to patient care
Does not sufficiently assess the patient to determine appropriate treatment (e.g. only assessing LOC to determine the need for Narcan)
Initiated protocol without proper indications (e.g. patient is not DLOC)
Does not perform an act that was required based on patient presentation that is potentially detrimental to patient care
Oxygen is administered by incorrect delivery device for patient presentation detrimental to patient care and/or
Positions the patient incorrectly with the potential to be detrimental to patient care (e.g. delaying sitting a patient who is dizzy or delaying putting a shock patient supine)

Performs an act that could aggravate the patient's condition or injury that is not already captured in the major performance criteria (e.g. excessively bumping a fractured leg which causes gross movement and pain)
Delays treatment and/or transport performing non-Priority tasks
Delays treatment and/or transport performing non-Priority tasks
Initiated protocol without proper indications (e.g. patient is not DLOC)
Fails to administer a medication indicated by the protocol not detrimental to patient care (e.g. Entonox for pain)
Does not complete baseline vital signs prior to initiating the protocol
Performs the protocol with isolated error with potential to be detrimental to patient care
Performs the protocol with isolated error with potential to be detrimental to patient care

notificationFacts.cc: acute confusion, fever and hypotension - suspected sepsis from a urinary source
notificationFacts.hxcc: normally fully oriented and independent; 48 hours of burning, frequency and almost no intake; acutely confused this morning; unwitnessed fall in the bathroom this morning while on apixaban
notificationFacts.vitals: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), BP 88/52, pulse 116 weak regular, resp 26 shallow, trunk hot and flushed with cool mottled peripheries and capillary refill 4 seconds, SpO2 92% on room air and 96% on 15 L, BGL 9.8, temp 38.7 tympanic; latest GCS 12, BP 84/50, pulse 122, resp 28, temp 38.9 - deteriorating
notificationFacts.treatments: high-flow oxygen, supine with blankets, spinal motion restriction for the unwitnessed fall, suction at the head; no glucose given (BGL 9.8); PCP: IV with fluid bolus en route; ETA 8 minutes
notificationFacts.findings: suprapubic tenderness, chest clear, no focal neurological deficit, no scalp injury found, pupils equal and reactive

handoffFacts.cc: acute confusion with fever and hypotension - suspected urosepsis
handoffFacts.hxcc: baseline fully oriented and independent with a walker; 48 hours of burning on urination, increased frequency and almost no oral intake; up all night, acutely confused this morning; unwitnessed fall in the bathroom this morning - unknown whether she struck her head - while on apixaban; two previous urinary infections that also presented as confusion
handoffFacts.initialVitals: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), BP 88/52, pulse 116 weak regular, resp 26 shallow, trunk hot and flushed with cool mottled peripheries and capillary refill 4 seconds, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 92% on room air and 96% on 15 L, BGL 9.8 mmol/L, temp 38.7 C tympanic
handoffFacts.finalVitals: GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), BP 84/50, pulse 122 weak regular, resp 28 shallow, trunk hot with cold mottled hands, pupils equal and reactive, SpO2 95% on 15 L, temp 38.9 C tympanic - deteriorating
handoffFacts.pmhx: hypertension, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis, mild cognitive impairment but oriented at baseline; two previous urinary infections
handoffFacts.meds: apixaban, bisoprolol (may blunt the heart-rate response), acetaminophen as needed
handoffFacts.treatments: oxygen at 15 L (SpO2 up to 95-96%), supine, blankets, spinal motion restriction for the unwitnessed fall, suction at the head; BGL 9.8 so no glucose given; medication list brought; rapid transport with early notification; PCP: IV with fluid bolus reassessed every 500 mL
handoffFacts.findings: suprapubic tenderness, chest clear, no focal neurological deficit, no scalp injury, pupils equal and reactive, dry mucous membranes and skin tenting, left hip bruise without shortening or rotation; last real intake 24 hours ago

pcrFacts.cc: Acute confusion, fever and hypotension in a previously oriented 82-year-old
pcrFacts.hxcc: 48 hours of dysuria, frequency and strong-smelling urine with almost no oral intake; acute confusion this morning; unwitnessed fall in the bathroom on apixaban; baseline per care aide is fully oriented and independent; two previous urinary infections presenting as confusion
pcrFacts.pmhx: Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis, mild cognitive impairment but oriented at baseline
treatments: Oxygen titrated to SpO2 94% or above (92% RA to 95-96% on 15 L)
Supine positioning to support blood pressure, blankets for warmth
Spinal motion restriction for the unwitnessed fall - NEXUS alertness criterion not met due to altered mental status
Suction at the head with a plan to tip the device if she vomits
BGL 9.8 measured - hypoglycemia excluded, oral glucose and glucagon correctly withheld
Temperature measured tympanically; medication list brought to hospital
RTC transport with early ED notification; IV fluids and antibiotics verbalized as out of EMR scope
findings: GCS 13 falling to 12 against a documented baseline of 15
Hypotension 88/52 falling to 84/50 with a weak pulse of 116 to 122
Hot flushed trunk with cool mottled peripheries and capillary refill of 4 seconds
Temperature 38.7 rising to 38.9; suprapubic tenderness; chest clear
No focal neurological deficit, no scalp injury found despite the unwitnessed fall on an anticoagulant
Dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor consistent with 24 hours of poor intake
pcrFacts.vitals: Set 1 (baseline on scene): GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), BP 88/52, P 116 weak regular, R 26 shallow, skin trunk hot flushed / peripheries cool mottled, CR 4 s, PERL, SpO2 92% RA and 96% on 15 L, BGL 9.8 mmol/L, T 38.7 C tympanic. Set 2 (en route, about 7 minutes later): GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), BP 84/50, P 122 weak regular, R 28 shallow, skin trunk hot / hands cold mottled, PERL, SpO2 95% on 15 L, T 38.9 C tympanic

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: She opens her eyes when you speak to her, mumbles "I'm fine dear... I'm fine" and drifts off again. She cannot tell you where she is or what year it is.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR runs this as a recognition-and-speed call: establish the baseline mental status from the aide, measure the blood glucose to exclude hypoglycemia and then correctly withhold glucose, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above (high flow - shock with altered LOC), supine positioning with blankets, spinal motion restriction because the confused patient fails the NEXUS alertness criterion after an unwitnessed fall, suction at the head, a temperature that supports the infective picture, and rapid transport with early notification. IV fluids and antibiotics are outside EMR scope - the EMR contribution is early recognition and a short scene time. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry and vascular access en route with a fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L, reassessed every 500 mL and titrated to a systolic of 90 - she is hypotensive with clinical signs of shock and 24 hours of almost no intake. Dimenhydrinate or ondansetron only if she vomits (she does not in this scenario), weighing the cautions in the elderly. Everything else is identical.

sourcePages: Scenario emd-05 (data/practical/emr-medical-1.json): dispatch, scene, primary (V on AVPU against a baseline of full orientation, shock with mottled peripheries, suprapubic tenderness, NEXUS fails on alertness), transport, history (care aide), vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions (glucose trap: BGL 9.8), ongoing (deteriorating GCS and BP), handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC; cool pale clammy skin secondary to suspected shock); p.11 primary-survey interventions (c-spine stabilization when NEXUS or Canadian C-Spine indicated; airway maintenance and suctioning in decreased LOC; oxygen for altered LOC and evidence of shock); p.13 AVPU; p.25 Spinal Management (NEXUS / Canadian C-Spine; manual stabilization, hard collar, spinal immobilization device, foam blocks; do not tape the head); p.50 Oxygen Administration (shock requires high-flow oxygen); p.54 Hypovolemia (supine, keep warm, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above; PCP: vascular access en route, fluid bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L reassessing every 500 mL); p.48 Nausea - Vomiting (PCP antiemetics only for nausea or vomiting; target systolic 90); p.57 Diabetic Emergencies (decreased LOC without a known cause; baseline vitals including BGL; glucose gel only with sufficient mentation; glucagon / D10W only for hypoglycemia); p.61 D10W; p.63 Dimenhydrinate (1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg; caution: elderly); p.67 Glucagon; p.75 Ondansetron (4 mg PO; CNS effects in the elderly); p.76 Oral Glucose (15 g PO; only with sufficient mentation to maintain an airway). Grading criteria p.19 (packaging goal times), p.35 (vitals intervals).
